title: Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI
extended_summary:
The paper addresses the challenge of teaching biomedical artificial intelligence in ways that are authentic, scalable, and responsible. Traditional problem-based learning (PBL) is well suited to biomedical engineering because it emphasizes real-world problem solving, teamwork, and interdisciplinary reasoning, but it is resource-intensive and difficult to keep current in rapidly changing AI domains. The paper asks whether a modular PBL framework augmented with guarded generative AI support can improve biomedical AI education while preserving critical thinking and ethical practice.

The intervention is a modularized PBL+AI curriculum in which student teams work through biomedical AI problem briefs, literature inquiry, project proposals, prototype development, model cards, final reports, and demonstrations. Generative AI tools are positioned as supports for literature navigation, knowledge summarization, coding assistance, debugging, reflection, and formative feedback, not as replacements for student reasoning. The framework includes explicit guardrails: approved-tool restrictions, privacy protections, AI-use disclosure, validation of AI outputs, source anchoring, code provenance marking, and equitable tool access.

The study was implemented over three academic years, 2021–2023, in biomedical AI-related courses at Georgia Tech and Emory University: Biomedical Health Informatics and Medical Image Processing at the graduate level, and Biostatistics at the undergraduate level. A total of 248 students participated, including 156 graduate students and 92 undergraduates, organized into 62 interdisciplinary teams. Outcomes were compared with historical pre-integration offerings from 2016–2017 and 2020, using grade distributions, peer evaluations, project deliverables, and student-authored publications as evidence.

The paper reports that AI-supported PBL cohorts showed higher proportions of A grades and fewer low grades than historical control cohorts, with the pattern remaining after excluding the pandemic-affected period. Student teams also produced 16 peer-reviewed publications, and peer evaluations indicated strong teamwork. The authors conclude that guarded GenAI integration can make PBL more scalable and implementation-focused in biomedical AI education, while noting that causal attribution is limited by the non-randomized historical design and the lack of student-level pre/post and long-term measures.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large-language-model assistants used as learning scaffolds for knowledge summarization, literature navigation, coding support, reflection prompts, formative feedback, and personalized guidance.
identified_tools.use_case: In biomedical engineering PBL courses, students used institutionally approved generative AI tools under guardrails for literature navigation and synthesis, coding initialization/optimization/debugging, reflection prompts, model-card and error-analysis support, and formative feedback while solving real biomedical AI problems.

findings.finding_summary: In historical cohort comparisons, AI-supported PBL offerings had higher A-rates than control offerings. Including the COVID-19 year, A-rates were 39.1% in Control vs. 66.4% in Intervention (Δ=+27.3 points; Welch t=4.28, p=0.042); excluding the COVID-19 year, A-rates were 39.1% vs. 67.4% (Δ=+28.3 points; Welch t=4.36, p=0.0367).
findings.effect_size: Δ=+27.3 percentage points including COVID-19 year; Δ=+28.3 percentage points excluding COVID-19 year

findings.finding_summary: AI-supported PBL offerings had fewer low grades than historical controls. Including the COVID-19 year, low-grade rates were 22.4% in Control vs. 6.1% in Intervention (Δ=-16.3 points; Welch t=-5.24, p=0.0076); excluding the COVID-19 year, rates were 22.4% vs. 4.25% (Δ=-18.12 points; Welch t=-6.93, p=0.0118).
findings.measure: Proportion of low grades (C or D/F)
findings.effect_size: Δ=-16.3 percentage points including COVID-19 year; Δ=-18.12 percentage points excluding COVID-19 year

findings.finding_summary: Mean GPA increased from 3.38 in Control offerings to 3.69 in Intervention offerings, but the difference was not statistically significant (Δ=+0.31; Welch t=2.30, p=0.142; 95% CI [-0.245, 0.865]). After excluding the COVID-19 year, GPA differences were directionally similar but still not significant (Δ=+0.325, p=0.130).
findings.effect_size: Δ=+0.31 GPA including COVID-19 year; Δ=+0.325 excluding COVID-19 year
findings.confidence_interval: 95% CI [-0.245, 0.865] including COVID-19 year; excluding COVID-19 year CI not_reported

findings.finding_summary: A 2 × 4 contingency analysis of year-averaged grade percentages across A/B/C/D–F indicated distinct grade profiles between Control and Intervention periods. The reported test was χ2(3)=22.30, p=0.0001, with Cramér’s V≈0.33.
findings.measure: Overall grade distribution across A/B/C/D–F categories

findings.finding_summary: During the 2021–2023 intervention period, student teams produced sixteen peer-reviewed publications in technical conferences addressing biomedical-AI problems. The paper presents this as evidence of high problem-solving productivity under implementation-focused, AI-supported PBL.

Peer evaluations were consistently high across the intervention courses. BHI peer evaluations ranged from 89.80% to 94.60%, MIP ranged from 88.80% to 90.60%, and undergraduate Biostatistics reported 94.24% in 2022 and 92.62% in 2023.
findings.measure: Peer evaluations of individual contributions, teamwork, and professionalism

findings.finding_summary: Within the AI-supported PBL context, exploratory student-level OLS analysis found that more coding experience was associated with higher performance. The reported slope was β=+1.88 points per year of coding experience, 95% CI [+0.30, +3.46], p=0.022.
findings.measure: Association between years of coding experience and score
findings.effect_size: OLS slope β=+1.88 points per year of coding experience

quality_tier_rationale: The study used a historical, non-randomized pre/post cohort comparison with descriptive and inferential analyses, not an RCT. The authors note attribution limitations, incomplete legacy enrollment data, and absence of student-level pre/post concept measures or rater-reliability estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported impacts were positive and practically large for grade distributions, including A-rate increases of about +27 to +28 percentage points, low-grade decreases of about -16 to -18 percentage points, and an overall grade-profile effect of Cramér’s V≈0.33. GPA gains were positive but not statistically significant.
